title: Meghalaya Launches ₹175 Crore 'Mission Golden Spice' to Turn Lakadong Turmeric Into a Global Luxury Brand
excerpt: The state government is backing its high-curcumin turmeric variety — grown exclusively in the Jaintia Hills — with processing infrastructure, GI tagging, and export incentives.
body:
• Meghalaya has launched the ₹175.45 crore 'Mission Golden Spice' initiative to develop Lakadong turmeric as a premium global brand
  • Lakadong turmeric, grown exclusively in the Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, contains up to 9% curcumin — roughly three times the level in common turmeric
  • The mission includes processing facilities, quality testing labs, GI tag protection, and direct export channels to premium markets
  • India produces about 80% of the world's turmeric but captures only a fraction of the premium market value chain

Meghalaya is betting big on a small, potent root. The state government has launched 'Mission Golden Spice,' a ₹175.45 crore initiative to transform its prized Lakadong turmeric from a locally traded commodity into a globally recognized luxury spice brand — aiming to capture a premium segment of the international market that has long eluded Indian turmeric producers.

What Makes Lakadong Special

Lakadong turmeric, named after the Lakadong area in Meghalaya's Jaintia Hills, is not ordinary turmeric. It contains up to 9% curcumin, the bioactive compound responsible for turmeric's anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. For comparison, most commercially available turmeric varieties contain 2-3% curcumin. That threefold concentration has made Lakadong a sought-after variety among health-conscious consumers, supplement manufacturers, and premium spice brands.

The turmeric is grown organically by indigenous Khasi and Jaintia tribal communities, predominantly women farmers, using traditional cultivation methods in the hilly terrain of northeastern India. The region's climate and soil conditions contribute to the variety's exceptional curcumin levels.

The Mission

Mission Golden Spice addresses every point in the value chain where Indian spice producers typically lose money. The initiative includes building modern processing facilities to convert raw turmeric into shelf-stable, export-ready products; establishing quality testing laboratories to certify curcumin content; pursuing a Geographical Indication (GI) tag to protect the Lakadong name; and creating direct export channels to premium markets in the US, Europe, Japan, and the Middle East.

India produces roughly 80% of the world's turmeric but captures only a fraction of the premium market value. Most Indian turmeric is exported as raw or semi-processed commodity, with the high-margin processing and branding done overseas. The Meghalaya government wants to change that equation for Lakadong.

From Farm to Global Kitchen

For the Indian diaspora, particularly health-conscious NRIs who have driven demand for high-curcumin turmeric supplements and golden milk powders in Western markets, the Lakadong story resonates. Many premium "turmeric supplements" sold in the US and Europe source curcumin from India but obscure the origin — and the farmers see little of the final retail price.

If Mission Golden Spice succeeds in building a recognizable Lakadong brand with certified curcumin levels and farm-to-shelf traceability, it could become a model for how Indian agricultural products can move up the value chain — something the country's vast farming sector has struggled to achieve at scale.
